### Core Rules

*Specialists consulted: systems-designer (primary), gameplay-programmer (feel/feasibility), engine-programmer (Godot 4.7.2 integration). Their one disagreement — tick rate — is resolved in CR-1. Items tagged **→ ADR** are engine-integration choices deliberately left out of this behaviour spec.*

**Vocabulary.** *Tick*: one fixed-step iteration of the authoritative simulation; tick number `T` is a monotonically increasing integer and the only clock the simulation knows. *State block*: a named, versioned, single-owner container of domain state registered with the kernel. *Command*: a serializable request to change state, carrying issuer identity. *Owner*: the domain system that is the only writer of a block. *Read view*: the read-only accessor an owner publishes. *Step hook*: owner-registered code that runs in the propagation phase. *Mode*: `HOST` (authoritative; the only mode in MVP) or `MIRROR` (VS-B guest: receives state, runs no authoritative tick) — the public API is identical in both. *PlayerId*: a stable seat identity (1 in single-player; PlayerId 0 is reserved as "no seat" — additive, provisional *(Amended 2026-10-27 — consistency pass, routed from ship-body-and-interior-physics)*); *peer_id*: the transport identity of a connection (host = 1). Persistent per-player state is keyed by PlayerId, never by peer_id, because peer IDs are reassigned per connection (this corrects the systems index's "keyed by peer ID" for Sanity and Suit).

**CR-1. Fixed tick at `TICK_RATE` = 60 Hz, with per-hook step divisors.** The simulation advances in steps of exactly `1/TICK_RATE` seconds of *simulated* time, independent of render frame time; durations everywhere are in ticks (the Attention tell window of 10–30 s is 600–1800 ticks). The kernel never reads wall-clock time or `delta`. Input- and physics-adjacent hooks run every tick; slow systems run at a divisor (Graph 6 → 10 Hz, Attention 6, Suit vitals 6, Sanity drift 12 → 5 Hz).
*Rationale and alternatives.* The gameplay-programmer argued for a 20 Hz kernel (slow systems don't need more; worst-case 50 ms latency is invisible behind immediate local acknowledgement) but set a hard floor of 15 Hz and would push back at 10. The engine-programmer argued for tick = physics rate so the moving ship body and the characters inside it share one timeline (*historical*: CR-1a later settled that the tick is driven from `_process`, not the physics step, and Body integrates ship-local kinematics inside the sim, so physics alignment is no longer a reason for any `TICK_RATE`) *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review)*. 60 Hz + divisors satisfies both: one clock, submit-to-applied within one tick (16.7 ms of simulated time) on an empty queue, and the cost profile of a 10 Hz graph. *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)* A variable timestep was rejected (breaks replay, tests and save equivalence); a 30 Hz kernel sits at a 2:1 ratio to the 60 fps render rate (alternate frames run 0 and 1 ticks), not at an awkward one to the physics step, which is not the clock. The tick *source* is settled in CR-1a (a `TickDriver` with an injected delta, not the physics callback); `step()` stays a plain method that tests and a future server call directly. Changing `TICK_RATE` later invalidates every tuned value expressed in ticks. *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)*

**CR-1a. Tick driver, clock source and catch-up** *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review; closes former Open Question 2, the technical-director confirms it in the spike)*. `Kernel.step()` has no clock. A `TickDriver` (a `RefCounted`, no scene tree) owns the accumulator, receives time as an injected integer count of microseconds (`delta_us`), and is driven by exactly one node with `process_mode = PROCESS_MODE_ALWAYS` from its `_process(delta)`; that node converts the engine's `delta` to `delta_us` once, and that conversion plus the diagnostics timer are the only wall-clock reads in the project (H9). **Godot's physics step is not the clock**: at MVP the avatar has no physics body (CR-13), so nothing needs the physics callback, and the driver needs no coupling to `physics/common/max_physics_steps_per_frame` (the former coupled constraint 4 is deleted). A later Vertical Slice physics projection runs in `_physics_process` as a `PROJECTOR` reading committed state and never steps the kernel. The accumulator is an integer in units of *microseconds × TICK_RATE*, so one tick is exactly `TICK_UNITS` = 1,000,000 units for every integer `TICK_RATE` (no float drift, no boundary flips); each frame that begins (after the boundary service) with the kernel `RUNNING` adds `acc += delta_us × TICK_RATE`. **Order of the add against the clear** *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review)*: the boundary service runs first; if it moved the kernel into `RUNNING` (a resume, a load, a finished save) the accumulator is cleared and **that frame's own `delta_us` is discarded** — the frame runs 0 ticks, because its wall time was spent paused, loading or saving — and the add applies from the next frame on; a frame that finds the kernel not `RUNNING` adds nothing. Per frame the driver (1) runs the boundary service (CR-15) before any tick; (2) while the kernel is `RUNNING`, runs `step()` `ticks_run = min(floor(acc / TICK_UNITS), MAX_TICKS_PER_FRAME)` times, **re-reading the kernel state after every `step()`** and stopping (and clearing `acc`) the moment it is no longer `RUNNING` — a P6 pause, a restore, a fault; (3) applies lag forgiveness (D.5); (4) flushes the result buffer (CR-5); (5) while `PAUSED`, runs the paused boundary service (CR-16). **The accumulator is cleared on every transition into `RUNNING`** (from `LOADING`, `PAUSED` or `SAVING`), so a load, an autosave or a pause never produces catch-up ticks afterwards. The driver node has a process priority that runs it before the presentation nodes, so presentation reads the tick the driver just produced. **Step 0 — input sample, and the priority table** *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review)*: nothing in the driver's step list sampled input, so the best-case latency of D.4 rested on an unstated ordering. The order inside one rendered frame is now fixed by process priority (lower runs first): **(0)** the input adapter (an `INPUT_SURFACE` object; it reads the engine's input state for this frame and calls `submit`, so its commands are admitted before the boundary service and the tick loop); **(1)** the `TickDriver` node (boundary service, then the tick loop, then forgiveness, result flush, paused service); **(2)** presentation nodes (Pixel-Perfect pipeline, HUD, Lighting, Audio), which read what the driver just committed. The adapter's priority is therefore strictly below the driver's number; a presentation node must sort after the driver (a lint on `process_priority` values; the engine reference is silent on ordering between nodes, so the spike verifies it, KRN-LAT-02). Tests call `Kernel.step()` directly, or inject `delta_us` into the driver; nothing in the kernel sleeps or reads a clock. **Main thread and `Engine.time_scale`**: the kernel, the driver and every owner callable run on the main thread only — no worker thread calls `submit`, a read view or a mutator (a lint forbids `Thread`, `WorkerThreadPool` and `call_deferred` into kernel code); `_process(delta)`'s `delta` is scaled by `Engine.time_scale` in the engine's contract as we read it (the pinned engine reference does not state it — **[UNV]**, verify in the spike), so release builds pin `Engine.time_scale = 1.0` (a boot check records `TIME_SCALE_NON_UNIT` in diagnostics otherwise) and a dev build that changes it knowingly scales simulated speed through `delta` — ticks stay exact integers either way.

**CR-2. Tick phase order.** Each tick executes these phases to completion, in order, with no interleaving:

| # | Phase | What happens | Who may write blocks |
|---|-------|--------------|----------------------|
| P0 | Begin | Tick counter increments; the pending set is *frozen* as this tick's candidate set (commands arriving now wait for T+1) | nobody |
| P1 | Intake | Candidate set in ordering-key order (CR-13) — a sort only when a non-monotone (remote) insert happened since the last tick, otherwise the head of an already-ordered queue — the first `MAX_CMDS_PER_TICK` form this tick's **batch**; the overflow returns to the unfrozen pending set in order and stays supersedable (Section E) | nobody |
| P2 | Dispatch | Per command in order: authority check → validate → apply or reject (CR-5) | the handler, inside `apply` only |
| P3 | Step | Step hooks in resolved order (CR-3); a hook runs when `T mod divisor == offset` | the hook's own block, plus owner-published mutators of other blocks (CR-9) |
| P4 | Commit | Dirty sets finalised; "tick committed" marker advances; interpolation baseline captured (`commit_baseline()` on each `interpolated` block — a kernel-run roll of a **derived presentation cache**, not a block write: the baseline is excluded from `snapshot()`, `canonical_bytes` and every hash, and is rebuilt by `snap_baseline` on every transition into `RUNNING`, so it has no canonical status and "nobody writes" stays true) *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review)* | nobody |
| P5 | Notify | Batched change notifications delivered (CR-10), then the result buffer is flushed (CR-5) | nobody — writes disabled |
| P6 | Boundary services | Pending control-plane requests in arrival order (CR-15), pending snapshot (Saving), command-log append | the kernel only |

P2 commands see earlier P2 effects in the same tick; P3 sees all of P2; subscribers and presentation only ever see post-P4 state, never a half-applied tick. **Paused service cycle** *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review; a retained seam that only test fixtures exercise at MVP, because no MVP command type sets `allowed_when_paused`)*: on every rendered frame while `PAUSED` the driver runs the paused boundary service — P1, P2, P4, P5, P6 with no P0 and no P3, `T` unchanged — dispatching only commands of `allowed_when_paused` types (CR-16). It is a deliberate carve-out from the running-tick guarantees: its commits apply at the current `T` (`apply_tick == queued_tick` is legal there, unlike a running tick), several commits can share one `T`, and G1/G2/G3 hold for it only as CR-13 states.

**CR-3. Step hooks and ordering.** Hooks register `(hook_id, owner, divisor, offset, after: [hook_id | {hook_id, tolerates_stale}])`. The kernel resolves a total order by topological sort of `after`; ties break by registration order, then `hook_id`. A cycle or unknown `hook_id` fails boot (CR-6). Sim-to-sim data flow within a tick is "reader declares `after` writer" (Suit vitals `after: graph.propagate.atmo` — the Graph registers three chained hooks, see its LS-1 *(Amended 2026-10-26 — consistency check, routed from the Life-Support Graph GDD)*). The order is data: testable, and printable by the Debug Overlay. An `after` edge between two hooks that never run in the same tick (Section E) must carry `tolerates_stale: true` if the reader accepts data up to a divisor old; boot warns only for **undeclared** mismatches, so the real boot (`horror.step` divisor 5 after `attention.step` divisor 6, the Graph's staggered chain — `.atmo` (6, 2) after `.power` (6, 0), `.failure` (6, 4) after `.atmo` — and the other cross-offset pairs of Section E) stays silent once declared and the warning keeps its meaning *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix)*. *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)* Hooks may not submit `PLAYER`-origin commands; they may submit `SYSTEM`-origin ones (CR-4) through `submit_system(type, payload, dedupe_key = none)` and may ask `has_pending(type, dedupe_key)` (CR-9 owner rule).

**CR-4. Command anatomy, origin and intents.** A command is plain serializable data:

| Field | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| `type` | Registered command type ID, owned by a domain system |
| `issuer_peer` | Stamped by the kernel's ingress — never taken from the payload |
| `origin` | `PLAYER` or `SYSTEM`, stamped by ingress |
| `actor` | The entity the command acts as: an opaque ID in the ID space of the type's declared `actor_source` block (CR-7; IDs are block-local, CR-8, so one number can name different entities in two blocks), or none *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix)* |
| `seq` | Monotonically increasing integer per `(issuer_peer, origin)` — the host's `PLAYER` and `SYSTEM` streams are separate spaces *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)*. **Stamped by the kernel at ISSUED, never chosen by a local caller**: every local `INPUT_SURFACE` handle and `submit_system()` receives the next value of the one kernel-held counter for its `(issuer_peer, origin)`, so any number of surfaces sharing the `(1, PLAYER)` space can never collide; the counter advances on every submit, including one rejected at admission, so locally stamped values are dense (1, 2, 3 …) and `DUPLICATE_SEQ` and gap counting apply only to a `seq` supplied by the **test ingress or a remote ingress** (the only two callers that may supply one) *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review, delegated ruling R2)* |
| `correlation` | Optional opaque `int` the submitting caller attaches (default 0 = none); the kernel never interprets it and echoes it unchanged in the command's result record and in any rejection event, so a caller (the Player Controller's pre-play tokens, a menu) matches a result to the act that caused it without learning or choosing `seq`. Kernel metadata like `submission_id`, never payload-borne; not part of `canonical_bytes` or any hash. Not unique: two submits may carry the same `correlation` *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review, delegated ruling R2)* |
| `payload` | Plain data only, per the recursive whitelist below; no object references, node paths or callables; `var_to_bytes(payload, false).size()` ≤ `MAX_PAYLOAD` |
| `queued_tick` | Stamped on enqueue |
| `submission_id` | Kernel metadata, never payload-borne: a kernel-unique counter stamped at ISSUED, before admission, so even a rejected submit has one; it is the `result_id` of the command's result (CR-5) *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)* |

*Discrete commands vs continuous intents.* If the sim must log, validate, save or replay it, it is a command (examples; each type's owner GDD is authoritative: Controller `set_move_intent`, `set_aim`, `toggle_beam`; Interaction `begin_cut` (module salvage, V8), `begin_patch`, `cancel_channel`, `pickup`, `drop`, `set_switch`, `field_check`; Modular Ship Assembly `begin_weld` (declared by Interaction, registered by Assembly), `begin_seam_cut`, `install_module` and the `SYSTEM`-only completions `weld` / `seam_cut` (registry: `assembly_commands`; there is no `remove_module` — it is reserved and unregistered, and V8 salvage is the only removal); Suit `equip_tool` (its only type); Web Map & Transit `pod_hop`, `berth`, `unberth` and the `SYSTEM`-only `pod_arrive`, `pod_settle`, `berth_step`, `web_reconcile` (registry: `web_commands`). `interact` is an input action, not a command type, and `use_item` has no owner and is not a command *(Amended 2026-10-27 — consistency pass, routed from interaction-system, suit-and-equipment, modular-ship-assembly and web-map-and-transit)*). What the stick is doing *right now* is an intent: intents are commands too, but a type may declare `coalesce = LATEST_PER_ACTOR_PER_TICK` — coalescing happens at admission over the unfrozen queue, keyed `(type, actor, issuer_peer)`, the older command becoming `Superseded` — and the input adapter sends one only when the quantised value changes — a few per second, never one per tick. Edge-triggered inputs (press, release, confirm) must declare `coalesce = NONE` or taps are lost. Movement integration runs inside the sim: Body's `body.integrate` hook (divisor 1, P3) reads the current intent and integrates ship-local kinematics (CR-13), so a move intent takes effect one tick after it is submitted, like every command; there is no physics-side integration at MVP, and position ownership is settled (Body owns it; the Controller owns intent and facing) *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)*. Under `STRICT_DEBUG` every command is round-tripped through serialization before dispatch, even locally; one that cannot survive is a violation (CR-19). **Submit is fire-and-forget and never calls back**: `submit()` returns nothing and invokes no callback, handler or subscriber, so it is safe to call from any handler, hook or result handler; its only outcome is one result record appended to the kernel's result buffer (CR-5), delivered at the next flush and identified by `result_id` — a remote issuer could never get a synchronous answer, so the local one doesn't either *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)*. `submit()` takes the optional `correlation` and returns nothing, not even a receipt: the caller learns the outcome only from the result record, which carries its `correlation` back, so "fire-and-forget" is literally true and `seq` stays the kernel's. The API shape is `submit(type, payload, actor = none, correlation = 0)` on an `INPUT_SURFACE` handle and `submit_system(type, payload, dedupe_key = none)` for hooks (a hook needs no correlation: it never receives a result) *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review, delegated ruling R2)*.

**Payload whitelist** *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)*. 'Plain' is a recursive `Variant.Type` whitelist checked at admission: `NIL`, `BOOL`, `INT`, `FLOAT` (finite only — `NaN` and `±inf` are `MALFORMED`; the same finite check applies to **each component of a `VECTOR2` and each element of `PackedFloat32Array`, `PackedFloat64Array` and `PackedVector2Array`**, which the walk visits in O(n) bounded by `MAX_PAYLOAD` *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review)*), `STRING`, `STRING_NAME`, `VECTOR2`, `VECTOR2I`, the `Packed{Byte,Int32,Int64,Float32,Float64,String,Vector2}Array` types, and `ARRAY`/`DICTIONARY` of the same, to a depth cap `PAYLOAD_MAX_DEPTH` = 8 (which also rejects a self-containing container). Dictionary keys must be `INT`, `STRING` or `STRING_NAME` and **all keys of one dictionary must share one type** (mixed keys have no canonical order, D.12). Anything else — an `Object`, `NodePath`, `Callable`, `Signal`, `RID`, a non-whitelisted `Variant.Type`, a non-finite float, a depth-9 nesting, mixed dictionary keys — is `MALFORMED`; the size bound is measured as `var_to_bytes(payload, false).size()` after the walk passes. Immediate *acknowledgement* (a tool sound, a hand animation, a linear progress bar starting) is presentation's job and happens in the same frame; the sim confirms on the next tick. The latency bounds are stated once, in Game Feel and D.4.

**CR-5. Command lifecycle and the exactly-one-result guarantee.** Every command reaches exactly one terminal state and emits exactly one result record (identified by `result_id`; delivered to its issuer unless it is `SYSTEM`-origin, see Result identity and delivery below). Stages: *Issued* → *Admission* (kernel state accepts commands; type registered; **origin allowed for the type — known at admission, so rejected there**; queue not full; `seq` not a duplicate — gaps are accepted and counted, not rejected; issuer rate limit; payload plain) → *Queued* → *Authority check* in P2 (origin re-checked as a defence in depth; if the type declares `actor_binding = OWNED_BY_ISSUER`, the binding table says the issuer controls the key `(actor_source, actor)` *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix)*; age ≤ the type's `max_age_ticks`) → *Validate* (owner's side-effect-free `validate(cmd, views, ctx)`: it reports through `ctx.ok()` or `ctx.reject(reason)` — a domain reason — and ends with `return ctx.complete()`; its return value carries no outcome, CR-19(a)/(b)) → *Apply* (`apply(cmd, write_scope, ctx)`, ending with `return ctx.complete()`; infallible by contract once validate passed, CR-9) → terminal: *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review, delegated ruling R3)*

| Terminal | Meaning |
|----------|---------|
| `Applied` | Effects are in state as of tick T (a command dispatched earlier in a tick that then faults is still `Applied`, with `detail.uncommitted = 1`) |
| `Rejected(reason)` | No effect |
| `Dropped(reason)` | Never evaluated: a reload, a shutdown or a fault flushed it — `RELOAD`, `SHUTDOWN`, `FAULTED` (the last added so G5 holds on the defect path). Includes the not-yet-dispatched commands of a faulting tick's batch *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)* |
| `Faulted(code)` | Evaluated, and its `validate` or `apply` (or a mutator it called) reported a fault through the fault channel (CR-19): effects may be partial and are unreachable to presentation. Exactly one command per fault — the cause. Distinct from `Rejected` (not 'no effect') and `Dropped` (not 'never evaluated') *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)* |
| `Superseded` | Coalesced away by a newer command of a coalescing type |

Kernel reject reasons are a closed set: `NOT_ACCEPTING`, `PAUSED`, `UNKNOWN_TYPE`, `QUEUE_FULL`, `RATE_LIMITED`, `DUPLICATE_SEQ`, `ORIGIN_NOT_ALLOWED`, `ACTOR_NOT_OWNED`, `STALE`, `MALFORMED`, `VALIDATION_FAILED(domain_code)` — domain codes are namespaced and owned by the registering system (Interaction's set, e.g. `OUT_OF_RANGE`, `INVALID_TARGET`, `PRECONDITION`, `BUSY`, is its GDD's). The result record carries `result_id`, `issuer_peer`, `origin`, `seq`, `correlation`, `ok`, `reason`, `subject` (the target the rejection refers to), an optional `detail` dictionary of numbers, and `tick` — **never display strings** *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review: `result_id` and `origin` added)* *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review, delegated ruling R2: `correlation` added, echoed unchanged from the submit)*. Presentation maps reasons to sound, shake or tooltip. **Reason codes are computed from true state and the kernel never filters them.** That is the whole of the kernel's claim. Whether, when and how cheaply a reason reaches the player is *not* the kernel's: Interaction, Sanity and the HUD own it and must obey Pillar 4's cost rule (a check costs time, risk or trust) — for example surfacing a `PRECONDITION` only after channel time has been spent, or only through diegetic feedback rather than an instant tooltip. *Design test (CD-GDD-ALIGN):* if a rejection lets the player falsify a hallucination at zero time, risk or trust cost, the presentation of that rejection is wrong — not the kernel. A command *aborted mid-channel* (power drops during a cut) is reported by the channel owner through state change, not through the command result. The kernel never retries.

**Result identity and delivery** *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)*. A result is identified by `result_id` (the command's `submission_id`). A local issuer correlates by the `correlation` it attached to the submit (echoed unchanged; the caller's own uniqueness, not the kernel's), never by `seq`, which a local caller neither chooses nor learns *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review, delegated ruling R2)*. `(issuer_peer, origin, seq)` is unique among results **except** `DUPLICATE_SEQ` rejections, which by definition repeat an earlier command's `(issuer_peer, origin, seq)` and are told apart by `result_id` and `reason`; only a test or remote ingress can produce one (see the `seq` row of CR-4). Every terminal result — admission rejections, `Superseded`, P2 results, `Dropped(...)`, `Faulted` — is appended to the kernel's **result buffer** in the order it occurs; `submit()` itself never delivers. The buffer is flushed (a) at P5 of every tick, after the change batch, and (b) by the driver once per rendered frame after that frame's ticks, **in every kernel state** (`BOOTING`, `LOADING`, `PAUSED`, `SAVING`, `FAULTED`, `SHUTTING_DOWN`, and an idle frame with no tick), so `NOT_ACCEPTING`, `PAUSED`, `Dropped(RELOAD|SHUTDOWN|FAULTED)` and every other result always have a delivery point. A flush swaps the buffer out before delivering: whatever a result handler submits (the STALE resubmit of Section E, for example) is admitted normally, and any result it produces lands in the fresh buffer and is delivered at the next flush, never recursively — a handler that resubmits on every rejection costs one result per flush and cannot loop. Results go to the issuing `INPUT_SURFACE`'s result handler and to the diagnostics log. **`SYSTEM`-origin results are never delivered to a subscriber or to the submitting owner** (owners never subscribe, CR-10); they go to the command log and the diagnostics counters only, and an owner that needs the outcome reads state. **Fault semantics (a designer decision, not an implementer detail)**: when the kernel faults, each command already dispatched in the faulting tick whose `apply` completed receives `Applied` with `detail.uncommitted = 1` (its effects are in the live blocks although P4 never ran); the faulting command receives `Faulted(code)`; every not-yet-dispatched batch command and every pending command receives `Dropped(FAULTED)`; all are buffered at the fault transition and delivered at the next frame flush.

**CR-6. Registration at boot, then frozen.** Block, command-type, hook, diagnostics-channel and binding-source registration are legal only in `BOOTING` *(Amended 2026-10-27 — consistency pass, routed from debug-overlay-true-values (E-DO-38))* (a block may declare one optional `binding_source` callable, CR-7; one registered after `BOOTING` is refused like every other registration *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix)*); after `BOOTING → LOADING` the registries are immutable until shutdown. Registration is an explicit declaration by the composition root, not discovery via the scene tree. Duplicate IDs, unknown types, missing owners and hook cycles fail boot loudly in every build. A command type registered without `allowed_origins`, `actor_binding`, `coalesce` or `max_age_ticks` (**no silent defaults**: an omitted `actor_binding` must never mean 'no ownership check'), a type with `actor_binding = OWNED_BY_ISSUER` but no `actor_source`, one whose `actor_source` names a block that registered no `binding_source`, and a `NONE` type that declares an `actor_source` (each fails boot with `ACTOR_SOURCE_INVALID`, naming the type) *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix)*, a block registered without `class`, `gameplay`, `repl_hint` or `persist`, a type whose `writes_blocks` names an unregistered block, and an `allowed_when_paused` type whose `writes_blocks` names any `gameplay = true` block likewise fail boot (`BOOTING → FAULTED`) naming the registration. *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)* A type with `coalesce ≠ NONE` that allows both origins fails boot (`COALESCE_DUAL_ORIGIN`), because the supersession key carries no origin (D.8); and the joint memory assertion of Section G constraint 8 is checked here *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review)*.

**CR-7. Authority model (behaviour).** The host is the sole authority: only a `HOST` kernel ticks and applies; a `MIRROR` never applies. Each command type's owner declares `allowed_origins ⊆ {PLAYER, SYSTEM}` and `actor_binding ∈ {NONE, OWNED_BY_ISSUER}` — both mandatory (CR-6) — and `allowed_origins` is checked at admission, with a P2 re-check as defence in depth. *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)* A type with `actor_binding = OWNED_BY_ISSUER` also declares **`actor_source`**: the `block_id` of the registered binding source whose ID space its `actor` belongs to (`body.state` for every avatar-acting type, `emitter.state` for `toggle_beam`). The P2 authority check passes iff `(actor_source(type), actor) ∈ half_b[PlayerId(issuer_peer)]`. So an actor and a beam with the same number can never stand in for each other. *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix)* `SYSTEM` commands never arrive from a network; remote ingress always stamps `PLAYER`. The kernel holds a **binding table** — `peer_id → PlayerId` and `PlayerId → {(source block_id, entity_id)}` — as identity data, not domain state; the table has two halves with different lifetimes *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix; Resolved 2026-10-28 — delegated ruling G6 (user delegated all remaining calls): the kernel owns the rebuild; closes Body Open Question 30)*. **(a) `peer_id → PlayerId`** is session state: it is mutated only through a host-only API called by the session owner (a boot step in MVP: `HOST_PEER_ID` 1 → PlayerId 1; Co-op Session in VS-B), and a restore, a death restart or a new game never touches it and never resets any issuer's `seq` or `last_seq`. **(b) `PlayerId → {(source block_id, entity_id)}`** *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix)* is derived from saved state and is never saved: **the kernel rebuilds it itself as the last step of every pass through `LOADING`** (`request_restore` and `request_new_game` alike), after the last `post_restore()` and the K-4 hash check and before the `LOADING → RUNNING` transition. The rebuild clears half (b) entirely, then calls each registered **binding source** (CR-6, CR-8) in ascending `block_id` order — with `ctx`, as a pure read of its owner's block, under no `WriteScope`, ending `return ctx.complete()` — which delivers `[(player_id, entity_id)]` in ascending order through `ctx.put`, and binds every pair under the source's own `block_id`: each delivered `(player_id, entity_id)` is stored as `player_id → (source_block_id, entity_id)`. Entity IDs are block-local (CR-8: each owner allocates from its own counter and the kernel allocates none), so the key always carries the source. Equal numbers from two sources (Body actor 1 and Emitter beam 1) are two different keys and never conflict. A key `(source_block_id, entity_id)` delivered for two different PlayerIds, or the same triple `(player_id, source_block_id, entity_id)` delivered twice, is `BINDING_REBUILD_CONFLICT`. A source that reports `ctx.fault` or returns without the sentinel is that source's fault. Either one takes `LOADING → FAULTED` naming the source. The checks compare keys only within one source. *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix; registry request: `kernel_binding_table` `half_b`, `errors`, `actor_source`, `referenced_by`)* Because `LOADING` is atomic within one boundary service, the rebuild is not a P6 control-plane request and no command can interleave with it; the P6 rule (Section E) governs session-owner changes to half (a) only. At MVP no binding source's pairs change during `RUNNING`, so no `RUNNING` tick sees an empty or stale half (b); a runtime seat or beam reassignment (VS-B) is a session-owner request honoured at P6 (Open Question 4, the co-op ADR). MVP binding sources: Body's `seat_bindings()` (its `SEAT` rows → `(seat, actor_id)`) and the Emitter's `beam_bindings()` (`(player_id, beam_id)`). Single-player: PlayerId 1 → {(`body.state`, avatar actor_id), (`emitter.state`, beam_id)}. Both numbers may be 1 (two independent counters), and the result is valid. *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix. Resolved 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix (G6): keyed by source rather than by namespace-tagged IDs, so Body's and the Emitter's persisted ID formats stay unchanged (G1).)* *(Alternative: Player Controller owns the binding as a block — rejected because the kernel could then not authority-check without calling a domain system. → ADR.)* **Single-player is not a special case**: local input is `PLAYER`-origin peer 1 (registry: `HOST_PEER_ID` = 1) acting on an entity peer 1 is bound to; the authority stage runs on every command from day one, so TD-FEASIBILITY's "authority discipline lapsing" risk is structural, not disciplinary. The kernel checks *who*; owners validate *whether the world allows it*; the kernel encodes no game rules. For friendly harm the kernel checks only issuer→actor ownership; the "attacker below the sanity threshold" gate is Interaction's `validate` calling Sanity's query on the actor's authoritative sanity level (a `SIM` block), never on anyone's perception.

**CR-8. State-block registry contract.** An owner registers: `block_id` (unique, namespaced, e.g. `graph.state`); `owner`; `schema_version` (bumped on any serialized-shape change); `class` ∈ {`SIM`, `PERCEPTION_OUT`} (CR-12); `persist` (false = derived, rebuilt after load) and, when true, `persist_scope` ∈ {`WORLD`, `PROFILE`} — `WORLD` blocks live in the world snapshot and roll back on `request_restore`; `PROFILE` blocks (decoded rules, lore, scars: Pillar 5's "never knowledge") live outside it and are never rolled back by a world restore; `scope` ∈ {`SHARED`, `PER_PLAYER` keyed by PlayerId}; `gameplay` (bool, mandatory: true when a gameplay verb can change the block; false only for settings, menu and save-request state — the CR-16 paused-write test) and `interpolated` (bool, default false: when true the kernel calls the owner's `commit_baseline()` at P4 so the previous/current pair rolls exactly once per tick, and after a restore or an owner-declared teleport/reset the owner calls `snap_baseline(key)` so presentation never interpolates across a discontinuity) *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)*; `repl_hint` ∈ {`HOST_ONLY`, `SHARED_SUMMARY`, `OWNER_PRIVATE`} — mandatory now though unused until VS-B, so no block ever ships without the decision; `snapshot(ctx)` (delivers its plain data through `ctx.put(payload)` and ends with `return ctx.complete()`; canonical state only, deterministic ordering, entity references by stable ID, no derived caches; **the payload is a deep copy** — `duplicate_deep()` for Dictionary/Array, `duplicate()` for Packed arrays, which GDScript passes by reference — never a reference into live state); `restore(data, stored_version, ctx)` (whole-block replace; **copies in** and never retains a reference to `data`, so two restores from one payload cannot alias; the owner migrates from `stored_version`; an unsupported version is a reported failure through the fault channel, never a silent default) *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)*; `default_state(ctx)` (when a save lacks the block; `ctx.put(state)`); `post_restore(ctx)` (after *all* blocks restore: resolve cross-block IDs, rebuild caches, check invariants); `read_view(ctx)` (the kernel's view-issuing surface calls it and hands the reader `ctx.put(view)`'s content: a getter-only facade or a copy — never a live container, CR-12); `commit_baseline(ctx)` and `snap_baseline(key, ctx)` for `interpolated` blocks; optionally `init_world(world_seed, ctx)` (a new-game step, CR-18); optionally `binding_source(ctx)` (delivers `[(player_id, entity_id)]` ascending through `ctx.put`; read only by the kernel's `LOADING` binding rebuild, CR-7) *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix)*. **Every one of these is a kernel-invoked owner callable, so every one receives `ctx`, returns only `ctx.complete()`'s token, and is never `-> void`** (CR-19(a)/(b)) *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review, delegated ruling R3)*. Restore order follows declared `restore_after`; a cycle in it, or a reference to an unregistered block, fails boot. *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)* Entity IDs are allocated by the owning block from a counter stored inside it; the kernel allocates none. An ID is therefore unique only within its block. Every cross-block reference the kernel holds (the binding table, CR-7) is keyed `(block_id, entity_id)`, and the kernel assumes no global ID space. *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix)* **No global RNG in simulation**: each system draws from a named stream whose counter lives in its block; the kernel supplies a pure derivation helper from `(world_seed, stream_name, counter)` and, for threat draws only, the epoch-keyed variant `rng_derive_epoch` (D.10) *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review, delegated ruling R1)*. The kernel's own clock (`kernel.clock`: tick counter + world seed, read through a view that also exposes `restore_epoch`) is its one registered block, class `SIM`, `persist = true` (scope `WORLD`; carried in the snapshot header as `T` and `world_seed`), **never marked dirty and never notifying** (`T` advances every tick; presentation reads it from the batch's `tick` and the read view), and excluded from the D.12 block fold because the hash prefix already covers `T ‖ world_seed`, so `T` is counted once *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)* — so a `PRESENTATION` subscriber (Failure & Trail) reads `world_seed` from its read view *(Amended 2026-10-27 — consistency pass, routed from failure-and-trail-system)* — and contains no domain facts. **`restore_epoch`** *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review, delegated ruling R1; the consequence of user ruling X8/D16, which this restates and does not reverse)*: Save/Load **owns** the value: a persisted `u32` starting at 0, held in the per-slot side file `slot_epoch.bin` (u32 + CRC32, written atomically by temp file + rename; in no generation file, whose headers keep only a read-only copy for recovery). It advances by 1 on every restore except one: a Continue of the newest non-demoted verified `QUIT` generation carries it unchanged, so a Save & Quit then Continue replays identical draws (user ruling D16). A death-stub restore, a `FAULT_RECOVERY` and a Continue of any other generation (after a kill, crash or fallback, in-process or after a fresh process start) advance it, and Save/Load makes the advance durable before it calls `request_restore` (CR-15) *(Amended 2026-10-28 — delegated ruling R1 as amended by R13/R14)*. The kernel receives it as an argument of `request_restore` and `request_new_game` (CR-15, CR-18), holds it read-only for the session and exposes it in the `kernel.clock` **read view** as the triple `(T, world_seed, restore_epoch)`, so a hook reads it purely, as a read of kernel state (H9). It is **not** part of the clock's canonical form, the snapshot header the kernel writes, the D.12 hash prefix or any hash: the hash prefix stays `T ‖ world_seed`, and the canonical keys stay `T` and `world_seed`, because the value is owned elsewhere and changes at every restore that advances it (CR-15) *(Amended 2026-10-28 — delegated ruling R13)*. The one derivation that uses it is the kernel's D.10 helper (`rng_derive_epoch`); no owner folds it by any other means. Blocks are typed data objects whose interchange form is plain data per H7, round-tripped through `var_to_bytes(..., false)` / `bytes_to_var` (Save/Load SL-2); a JSON dump is diagnostic only, and any 64-bit value above 2^53 (`world_seed`, `T`, `state_hash`, per-block hashes, RNG counters) crosses it as a `hex64` string (owned by Save/Load; registry: `hex64`), never as a JSON number *(Amended 2026-10-27 — consistency pass, routed from save-load-and-versioned-format (K-3))* (→ ADR for Resource vs RefCounted); every block has a round-trip test. **4.7 gotcha (sourced)**: writing one element of a packed array no longer fires the property setter, so dirty-tracking must be explicit in mutation methods, never in setters.

**CR-9. Write discipline and atomicity.** A block is written only by its owner's mutators, and only inside a `WriteScope` the kernel issues during P2 apply or P3 step; outside those phases a mutator is refused in every build (no write, no dirty key), increments `WRITE_OUTSIDE_SCOPE` and reports a violation (CR-19). *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)* **Cross-block commands** (weld, cut, module install, pod hop) call *public mutators* other owners explicitly publish; the kernel guarantees the whole `apply` is atomic against every other command, hook and snapshot, followed by one notification batch. **Failure model: validate-then-apply, no rollback.** `validate` proves everything through read-only queries (for weld, the Graph's pure join-validation query); `apply` is infallible by contract; a failure inside `apply` — reported through the fault channel, never by throwing or asserting (CR-19) — is a defect that moves the kernel to `FAULTED` (C.2). *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)* *(Copy-on-write rollback rejected for MVP cost; event sourcing rejected as primary store — the kernel keeps a bounded command log for diagnostics and replay tests only.)* Step hooks affect other systems by (a) a published unconditional mutator (a horror writing a footprint into the Graph's footprint channel) or (b) a `SYSTEM`-origin command processed at T+1 when the target may reject. The kernel enforces *phase*; "only declared callers call declared mutators" is enforced by lint and the control manifest. → ADR

**Owner rule for `SYSTEM`-submitting hooks** *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)*. The pending queue is kernel data, not a block, so it is not in a snapshot, and a `SYSTEM` rejection is invisible to hooks (results go to the log only). A hook that submits `SYSTEM` commands (Assembly's `weld` / `seam_cut` completions, Transit's `pod_*`, Horror) must therefore be **restart-safe and rejection-tolerant**: its decision to submit is a function of persisted state, so after a restore (pending queue empty, `Dropped(RELOAD)`) it simply decides again; the completions are idempotent; timeouts are expressed in state (`submit_T + PENDING_TTL_TICKS + 1`), never as 'wait for the result'. A divisor-1 hook must guard re-submission with `has_pending(type, dedupe_key)` (or a `dedupe_key` on `submit_system`), because while the queue is backlogged it would otherwise queue a duplicate every tick. G4 (CR-13) holds only for owners that obey this rule.

**CR-10. Change notification contract.** Notifications are emitted once per tick in P5, after commit, batched per block as `(block_id, tick, change_keys)`; if more than `MAX_DIRTY_KEYS` changed, `change_keys` collapses to `ALL`. **Payloads carry no state**; subscribers fetch through read views, so notifications are identical whether state arrived by command (`HOST`) or by replication (`MIRROR`) and presentation never changes between modes. Subscriber classes are declared at subscribe time:

| Class | May do | Examples |
|-------|--------|----------|
| `PRESENTATION` | Read `SIM` and `PERCEPTION_OUT` views; write only CanvasItem / Material / Light2D / particle / audio nodes | Failure & Trail, Instruments, HUD, Lighting, Perception Filter, Audio |
| `INPUT_SURFACE` | As `PRESENTATION`, plus **submit** commands as the local seat | Player input adapter, Chart Table, menus |
| `PROJECTOR` | Same reads; write engine-side *derived* objects owned by its block owner (physics shapes, bodies, scene content); never writes blocks | Body's Vertical Slice physics shapes (at MVP the Layout's integer footprint rectangles are SIMULATION data read by Body's `LocomotionStep` and the Emitter's segment test; the avatar has no physics body *(Amended 2026-10-27 — consistency pass, routed from ship-section-and-layout-data-model)*); derelict content build |
| `REPLICATION` | Read views marked for replication; send | Co-op adapter (VS-B) |
| `DIAGNOSTIC` | Read everything, including kernel internals | Debug Overlay |
| *(none for SIM)* | An object that **owns a block or a hook** never subscribes; sim-to-sim is ordered step reads or commands. The rule is per subscriber *object*, not per system: Player Controller's input adapter and Interaction's prompt object are separate objects that subscribe as `INPUT_SURFACE` (they own no block and no hook) *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)* | — |

Subscriber handlers run with writes disabled. Render `PRESENTATION` gets no submit API; `INPUT_SURFACE` is the one class that may submit, which is how "presentation never writes simulation" coexists with menus that issue commands. *(The `INPUT_SURFACE` and `PROJECTOR` readings of the TD rule are provisional pending a technical-director ruling — Open Questions.)* **Sim never calls presentation**: the flow is always state → notification → presentation. Horror light disturbance and Attention flicker are state that Lighting reads, not calls into Lighting. There are two consumer channels: true values (Debug Overlay only) and filtered values (the Perception Filter reads true state and publishes what a client perceives; presentation nodes read the filtered channel). The kernel exposes `tick_alpha` for render interpolation; owners of moving state expose previous and current committed values in their read views. → ADR for transport (signals vs registry). **Catch-up delivery** *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review; ratified 2026-10-27 — user ruling (design-review decisions), R-12, Open Question 21 resolved)* *(Amended 2026-10-27 — user rulings)*: in a frame that runs more than one tick, `PRESENTATION`, `PROJECTOR` and `DIAGNOSTIC` batches are delivered once, after the frame's last tick, with `tick` = that tick and `change_keys` = the union of the frame's ticks (collapsing to `ALL` past `MAX_DIRTY_KEYS`), because presentation only ever reads the last committed state and N intermediate batches are wasted work; `INPUT_SURFACE`, `REPLICATION` and control-plane callers still receive every tick's batch, and the result buffer is flushed every tick. Ticks stay atomic (G6); only the delivery of a presentation batch is merged. **Delivery on an early exit from the loop** *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review)*: if the loop stops early (a P6 pause, a restore, a fault), the merged batch covers **committed ticks only** — the union of the `change_keys` of ticks whose P4 ran — and is delivered at the exit, after the state change is visible to the driver; a fault delivers nothing for the faulting tick (P4 never ran) and merges nothing, and a restore delivers `ALL` for every block to every subscriber class (the world was replaced) once the kernel is `RUNNING` again. **Subscriber lifetime** *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review)*: `subscribe(class, handler)` returns a **subscription handle**; `handle.unsubscribe()` removes it, and the kernel also checks `handler.is_valid()` before each call and prunes a freed subscriber (counter `DEAD_SUBSCRIBER`, not an error and not `INCOMPLETE`), so a freed HUD or Chart Table node never raises an engine error that would be misreported. P5 iterates a **snapshot of the subscriber list taken before P5 begins**, so a handler that subscribes or unsubscribes during delivery affects the next tick only. `Kernel.dispose()` (idempotent) unsubscribes everything, drops the registries and breaks the `RefCounted` cycles between kernel, driver and handles, so a test kernel is freed deterministically (no leaked instances at test end).

**CR-11. Time model for presentation.** Presentation runs at render rate and reads last-committed state. It never causes a tick; pausing presentation effects (reduced motion) never pauses the sim.

**CR-12. Perception isolation, enforced by block class.** `SIM` blocks are readable by simulation code and presentation. `PERCEPTION_OUT` blocks (Sanity's per-player "what lies to show" output) are *write-only to simulation*: no sim code — including the owner's own hooks — obtains a read view; presentation and the replication adapter do. Sanity's drift and the friendly-harm gate read the sanity *level* (`SIM`), never the perception block. A sim-side read of a `PERCEPTION_OUT` view is refused in every build: it returns an empty view, increments `PERCEPTION_READ_BLOCKED` and reports a violation (CR-19). *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)* Perception state is `persist = false` by default (rebuilt from the sanity level and the persisted `sanity.ledger`) *(Amended 2026-10-27 — consistency pass, routed from sanity-and-hallucination-rules (C19))* and `OWNER_PRIVATE` in VS-B.

**Read views are getter-only facades or copies, and the guarantee is 'structural plus tripwire'** *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)*. GDScript has no const references: a `Dictionary`, `Array` or Packed array returned from a view is a live container any reader could write to. A read view therefore returns either a facade exposing getters only (indexed access into the owner's storage, for large blocks such as the Graph) or a copy (`duplicate_deep()` / `duplicate()`, for small blocks) — never the owner's live container. What the kernel enforces *structurally* is the issuance surface: `WriteScope` exists only in P2/P3, `PRESENTATION` and `PROJECTOR` receive no submit handle, and owners register no subscription. What it can only *detect* is a reader that mutates a container it should not hold: under `STRICT_DEBUG` the kernel hashes the `SIM` blocks (uncached, so a write that bypassed the dirty bit is seen) **once per dispatch batch** (before the batch's first `validate` and after its last — a `validate` that mutated is caught as a changed hash across the batch and named by block, which is coarser than per-command and is the cost trade) **and once around P5**, and a changed hash is a `SIM_WRITE_TRIPWIRE` violation naming the block *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review; the earlier "around each `validate`" cost up to 129 uncached encodes per tick and made the dev profile unplayable during a burst)*. The tripwire is the only detector for a missed dirty mark, so its **coverage may not shrink**: these per-tick hashes run under a wall-clock budget cap (`TRIPWIRE_BUDGET_MS`, dev only, **[PLACEHOLDER]** 1.0 ms per tick; blocks over the cap are deferred, never skipped), and **every `SIM` block is swept at least once every `TRIPWIRE_SWEEP_TICKS` ticks (**[PLACEHOLDER]** 60) wherever the budget deferred it**; the test profile ignores the budget and always hashes uncached around every batch and P5 *(CD resolution of the tripwire disagreement)*. H3/H4 are thus enforced by structure, lint and tripwire together, not by structure alone.

**CR-13. Determinism and ordering guarantees** (`HOST` mode, same build and platform). **G1 Order**: commands apply in ascending `(queued_tick, host_order)`; in single-player that is submission order. *Carve-out (paused service cycle, CR-2)*: commits there are ordered by the same key but at the frozen `T`. *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)* **G2 Single timeline**: every command applies at exactly one tick (a paused-cycle commit applies at the current, frozen `T`; running-tick commands satisfy `apply_tick ≥ queued_tick + 1`). *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)* **G3 Replay**: from an initial snapshot, the same `PLAYER` command stream, the same *recorded physics observations* and the same **control-plane request log** (each request with the boundary at which it was honoured, including any paused cycle's `host_order` keys, the `restore_epoch` each restore or new game installed, and every accepted or refused runtime `set_knob` change with its boundary) yield identical block state at tick N (canonical snapshot hash), **given `(save bytes, restore_epoch)`**: the same pair replays identically and a different epoch changes exactly the epoch-keyed threat streams (D.10) and nothing else *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review, delegated ruling R1)*. **The log's format and owner**: the kernel emits one diagnostic *request event* per control-plane request and per admitted `PLAYER` command `(kind, boundary = (T, phase or frame-boundary), host_order, payload digest)`; a **test-side recorder** subscribed as `DIAGNOSTIC` collects them into the replay stream. The `COMMAND_LOG_CAPACITY` ring buffer is a diagnostics aid with eviction and is **not** the replay source *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review)*. *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)* **G4 Save equivalence**: snapshot at T, restore, continue ≡ uninterrupted play for `persist` blocks (hash-compared) — the key regression test for CR-8. *Preconditions*: (1) every `SYSTEM`-submitting hook obeys the CR-9 owner rule (the pending queue is not saved, so a `SYSTEM` command queued at tick T's P3 is absent after a restore at T; a restart-safe hook resubmits from state); (2) **no `PLAYER` command is pending at the capture boundary** — pending commands are not in the snapshot and are `Dropped(RELOAD)` by the restore, so a capture with a non-empty queue is not equivalent to uninterrupted play; the harness captures at a boundary where the queue has drained (it submits nothing on the preceding tick), and the **remaining command stream** is then defined as the recorded `PLAYER` commands admitted **after** that boundary, fed to both runs; (3) the restored run and the control run use the **same `restore_epoch`** (tests pin it; the control run's epoch is the one the restored run was given), because a different epoch deliberately changes threat draws *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review; re-review, delegated ruling R1)*. **Cross-platform note**: G1–G4 are guaranteed on the same build and platform only; a save written on another platform or build that reports `match = false` in the K-4 verdict is expected where any `SIM` state is float-valued, not a kernel defect, and Save/Load's REBASED policy must treat it so *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review)*. **G5** exactly-one-result (CR-5). **G6 Atomic ticks** (CR-2). Physics-derived facts (positions after collision, contacts, raycasts) are *inputs* from the engine: Godot Physics 2D makes no determinism claim, so G3 either records and replays them or excludes physics-coupled blocks. This is a stated limit, not a defect; host-authoritative co-op needs host truth, not cross-machine lockstep. In the MVP no block is physics-coupled: Body's `body.integrate` hook integrates ship-local integer kinematics and samples nothing (the avatar has no physics body), so G3 needs no recorded observations and Open Question 5 is moot for the MVP *(Amended 2026-10-27 — consistency pass, routed from ship-body-and-interior-physics (BDY-3))*. → ADR

**CR-14. Hard rules** — each becomes a lint, a test, or a control-manifest line. **H1** No domain state in the kernel (kernel-owned data is exactly: `kernel.clock`, the command queue, the registries, the binding tables, the command log, kernel state, diagnostics). **H2** No kernel-defined domain commands; its control plane (CR-15) is a host-local API, not commands. **H3** One owner per block; writes only via owner mutators inside a `WriteScope`. **H4** Presentation never writes simulation; render presentation has no submit API. **H5** No simulation system reads perception state. **H6** Peer identity on every command, kernel-stamped, never payload-borne; a command constructor without `issuer_peer` must not exist. **H7** Everything crossing the kernel boundary is plain data. **H8** No networking code in MVP: the only ingress is local input, the only egress local presentation. **H9** Simulation never reads wall-clock or global RNG. **H10** Kernel logic is scene-tree independent — runs headless, testable without a scene; a `Kernel.step()` call advances the sim synchronously in tests. Autoload vs node → ADR; if an autoload exists it is a thin holder of an instance that code receives as a parameter, so tests never share global state.

**CR-15. Control plane** (host-local, not commands): `request_pause`, `request_resume`, `request_snapshot`, `request_restore`, `request_new_game` *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review; CR-18)*, `request_shutdown`. Callers: Save/Load, the pause/Chart Table UI (host-local call), boot code. **Timing** *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)*: a request is recorded when made — from any phase, from a hook, from a P5 handler, or from outside a tick (a UI call between frames) — and served at the **next boundary**, where a boundary is the P6 of a tick or the driver's per-frame boundary service (run before any tick of the frame and, while `PAUSED`, every frame), whichever comes first; the call itself never changes state. `request_shutdown` is accepted from **every state except `SHUTTING_DOWN`** (including `BOOTING`, `LOADING` and `SAVING`; in those it is served at the boundary that follows the atomic step). Requests reaching the same boundary are applied in arrival order, never coalesced: a `request_pause` then a `request_resume` on one boundary leaves the kernel `RUNNING` with no paused service cycle run; a caller that needs a definite state re-issues the state it wants (Chart Table CT-4) *(Amended 2026-10-27 — consistency pass, routed from chart-table-web-map-and-menus (ASK-CT-9))*. **`request_restore(payload, restore_epoch, expected_state_hash = none)`** (K-4) *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review, delegated ruling R1; amended 2026-10-28 — delegated ruling R1 as amended by R13/R14: `restore_epoch` is supplied by Save/Load, whose epoch staging step has completed before the call is made: `EPOCH_DURABLE`, or a logged `SL_EPOCH_NOT_DURABLE` with `save_status = FAILED`, or no advance was due. Save/Load advances the value on every death-stub restore, every `FAULT_RECOVERY` and every Continue except one of the newest non-demoted verified `QUIT` generation, which carries it unchanged and writes nothing (R13). The kernel never waits on that write: no Save/Load I/O completes inside `LOADING`, which stays atomic within one boundary service (States). **Listed exposure (failure path, R14):** after `SL_EPOCH_NOT_DURABLE` the installed epoch exists only in Save/Load's memory, so a process kill before Save/Load's next successful epoch write may replay that epoch once; G3/G4 are unaffected because they are defined given the `(save bytes, restore_epoch)` pair. The kernel holds it read-only for the session, exposes it in the `kernel.clock` read view (CR-8) and rejects a value outside the u32 range in its pre-check, `RESTORE_EPOCH_RANGE`)*: when an expected hash is given, the kernel recomputes `state_hash(PERSIST, T)` (D.12) after the last `post_restore()`, inside `LOADING` and before the first `RUNNING` tick, and reports `{T, computed_hash, match}` to the requester; Save/Load derives its EXACT / REBASED / mismatch verdict from it (SL-12). A mismatch is **not** a `FAULTED` transition — release plays on; policy is the requester's. Save/Load does not use restore-into-`PAUSED` for this window *(Amended 2026-10-27 — consistency pass, routed from save-load-and-versioned-format (K-4))*. **Control-plane read access:** a control-plane caller is not one of the CR-10 subscriber classes; Save/Load (the one such caller at MVP) may read `kernel.clock`, the Controller's per-seat `loco_state`, the Graph's `read_view.failures()` and an optional Attention `SIM` read view, and receives end-of-tick notifications, all read in the tick boundary in which it issues a request; it never reads `PERCEPTION_OUT`, never submits commands and never holds a `WriteScope` *(Amended 2026-10-27 — consistency pass, routed from save-load-and-versioned-format (SL-13))*. In VS-B a guest's pause or save *request* is a command defined by Session or Save/Load, validated on the host, which then calls the control API.

**CR-16. Pause semantics.** `PAUSED` stops the tick but not rendering. While paused, submit accepts only types flagged `allowed_when_paused` by their owner, and **only non-diegetic actions may carry the flag** (save, settings, resume, menu navigation) — no gameplay verb that changes `SIM` state is allowed while paused, so a solo player cannot equip, repair or re-route with time stopped mid-tell (Dread Before Chaos), and solo pause behaves like co-op's overlay-only pause; a paused-allowed command may write only blocks registered `gameplay = false` **and** named in the type's `writes_blocks` (boot-checked, CR-6; the `WriteScope` issued in the paused cycle carries exactly that set, and a write outside it is refused and counted as `WRITE_OUTSIDE_SCOPE`), never a `SIM` gameplay block *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)*; everything else is rejected `PAUSED` immediately, never queued, so there is no burst on resume. Admitted paused-allowed commands are dispatched by a **paused service cycle** that runs P1, P2, P4, P5 and P6 with no P3 and with `T` unchanged, **once per rendered frame while `PAUSED`** (the paused boundary, which also serves control-plane requests), so a save or a menu action takes effect without advancing simulated time. At MVP no command type sets the flag; the cycle is a retained seam that only test fixtures exercise (CR-2). *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)* Commands already queued when the pause is honoured are neither dispatched by the service cycle nor rejected: they wait, in order, for the first `RUNNING` tick after resume. **Pause is single-player only**: in co-op a menu cannot stop a shared sim — VS-B treats pause as a UI overlay with the kernel `RUNNING`. The Chart Table GDD must not assume "pick a target" happens while paused. Relationship to the scene tree's pause → ADR.

**CR-17. Bounds and overload behaviour.** At most `MAX_CMDS_PER_TICK` processed per tick, the rest waiting FIFO. `QUEUE_CAPACITY` total and `PER_ISSUER_CAPACITY` per issuer; beyond that `QUEUE_FULL` at admission — never silent drop, never unbounded growth. Catch-up runs at most `MAX_TICKS_PER_FRAME` ticks per frame, then lets simulated time lag rather than spiral (lag above `LAG_FORGIVE_TICKS` is dropped at the end of the frame, D.5); a lag counter is exposed to diagnostics. P3 exceeding `STEP_BUDGET_MS` logs the slowest hooks but the tick completes. A command older than its type's `max_age_ticks` is rejected `STALE`, so a hitch cannot unleash a second of stale intents. At the defaults `STALE` is unreachable from local ingress (the queue can hold a command at most 8 ticks and `T` does not advance while paused or saving); it is a VS-B seam for remote-stamped ticks, guarded locally by a "never stale" invariant test (Section E; ratified 2026-10-27 — user ruling, R-3). *(Amended 2026-10-27 — user rulings)*

**CR-18. Snapshot semantics.** A snapshot is taken only at a tick boundary (P6), covers all `persist` blocks at the same T, and records `(T, per-block schema_version)`. Capture is synchronous and in memory with the tick halted (`SAVING`), and **atomic within a single boundary service — `SAVING` never spans a frame**; file I/O is Save/Load's and off the critical path → ADR. *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)* Restore replaces all `WORLD`-scoped persisted blocks atomically and leaves `PROFILE`-scoped blocks untouched (Pillar 5: losing the ship or a body never loses knowledge); partial restore within a scope is unsupported; failure aborts to `FAULTED` with pre-restore state intact where possible. With join-in-progress deferred, the same snapshot/restore contract is VS-B's guest transfer at session start, so it must be complete and cheap. **New game (K-2):** a new game passes through `LOADING`: every block takes `default_state()`, Save/Load's `new_game(world_seed)` sets `world_seed` into `kernel.clock` *(a new game is entered by the control-plane call `request_new_game(world_seed, restore_epoch = 0)`, valid from `BOOTING` (the first boot, States table), `RUNNING`, `PAUSED` and `FAULTED` *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix)*, so a second new game in one process — for example "death = restart from the last autosave" when no autosave exists yet — has a path; it flushes the queue with `Dropped(RELOAD)` exactly like `request_restore`, resets `T` to 0, installs the supplied epoch (a fresh slot's `slot_epoch.bin` starts at 0, Save/Load SL-18, SL-23; amended 2026-10-28 — delegated ruling R14) and leaves `PROFILE`-scoped blocks untouched: Pillar 5, a new world never loses knowledge; what a new crew keeps is Open Question 13, Save/Load's) (Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review)*, then each owner that registered an `init_world(world_seed)` step runs it in `restore_after` order under one `WriteScope`, before `post_restore()`; at MVP the world build is Web Map & Transit's `init_world` (WM-7), which calls the Layout, Graph and Body mutators in its fixed order *(Amended 2026-10-27 — consistency pass, routed from save-load-and-versioned-format (SL-18) and web-map-and-transit)*. The last step of every pass through `LOADING`, restore or new game, is the CR-7 binding rebuild (after the `init_world` steps and `post_restore()`, and after a restore's K-4 hash check), so the first `RUNNING` tick already sees the rebuilt `PlayerId → {(block_id, entity_id)}` half *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix)*.

**CR-19. Fault channel, violations and build profiles** *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review; replaces the earlier 'throws / asserts' model)*. GDScript has no `try`/`catch`: a runtime script error is printed by the engine, aborts the function it occurred in and hands control back to the caller with a default value the caller cannot distinguish from a result; and `assert()` is compiled out of release exports. The kernel therefore **never relies on an exception or an assertion for control flow**, and every behaviour in this document is identical in debug and release unless a clause calls it a `STRICT_DEBUG` extra.
- **(a) Fault channel and the one callable contract** *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review, delegated ruling R3; defines the contract once)*. **Kernel-invoked owner callables** are a closed list: `validate`, `apply`, step hooks, `snapshot`, `restore`, `post_restore`, `default_state`, `read_view`, `commit_baseline`, `snap_baseline`, `init_world`, and the result- and subscriber-handlers. The kernel calls each through `Callable.call()` and passes a context object as the last argument (`ApplyContext`/`WriteScope`, `HookContext`, `SnapshotContext`, `NotifyContext`). **Results flow through `ctx`, never through the return value**: `validate(cmd, views, ctx)` reports through `ctx.ok()` or `ctx.reject(reason)`; `snapshot(ctx)`, `default_state(ctx)` and `read_view(ctx)` deliver their payload through `ctx.put(payload)`; `apply(cmd, write_scope, ctx)`, hooks, `restore`, `post_restore`, `init_world`, `commit_baseline`, `snap_baseline` and handlers report only success-by-completion; every callable reports failure with `ctx.fault(code, detail)`. **Every callable's only return statement is `return ctx.complete()`** (a typed token, (b)); no owner callable is declared `-> void`, because a `void` GDScript function cannot return the token and the engine's default for an aborted typed function would alias a legitimate result. A `validate` that calls neither `ok()` nor `reject()` is `Faulted(NO_OUTCOME)`; the first outcome call stands and a second is a violation (`CTX_DOUBLE_OUTCOME`). **Published mutators are not on this list**: other owners, not the kernel, call them, so the kernel cannot check their sentinel; they take the shared `WriteScope`, report with `scope.fault(code, detail)` and return a status that callers propagate — which is also why the sentinel's blind spot (below) is closed by status propagation. The kernel checks `ctx.faulted` (which includes any fault a mutator reported on the shared scope) and the completion token after **every** kernel-invoked call, before using its result. A fault in `apply`, a hook, `snapshot`, `restore`, `post_restore`, `init_world`, `default_state`, `commit_baseline` or `snap_baseline` (and in a mutator they called) moves the kernel to `FAULTED`; **a fault in `read_view` never does**: views are obtained by presentation at render time, outside any tick, and a HUD read must not be able to halt the ship (CR-11, H4) — it is recorded and counted (`INCOMPLETE` or the violation, as a P5 handler's is), the reader receives an empty view, and when sim code called it inside P2/P3 the enclosing `apply` or hook fails through the status it propagates; a fault reported by `validate` does not reject, it faults (a defect), whereas `ctx.reject(reason)` is the ordinary domain rejection (`Rejected(VALIDATION_FAILED(reason))`, kernel stays `RUNNING`); a fault in a P5 or result handler is recorded and counted but cannot fault the kernel (the tick is committed).
- **(b) Completion sentinel.** The kernel arms `ctx.completed = false` and a fresh `ctx.token` before each call; `ctx.complete()` sets `completed` and returns that token — a typed, non-nil, non-zero object (a per-call `CompletionToken` instance) that the kernel compares **by identity**, so a `null`, `0`, `false` or empty value returned by an aborted or forgetful function can never read as success. A call that returns anything but the armed token with `completed` set (the script aborted on an engine error, or forgot) is `fault(INCOMPLETE)` for `apply`, hooks, `validate`, `snapshot`, `restore`, `post_restore`, `default_state`, `commit_baseline`, `snap_baseline` and `init_world`, and a recorded `INCOMPLETE` diagnostic, without a fault, for a P5 or result handler and for `read_view` (which returns an empty view). In a release build the sentinel is the only abort guard (`assert` is compiled out), so it is exercised on a release export in the spike (Acceptance Criteria, KRN-CTX-06). The sentinel catches a *function that aborted*; it cannot catch an error in a nested helper that the outer function then ignores — which is why mutators also return statuses and callers must propagate them.
- **(c) What cannot be done.** Engine script errors cannot be intercepted. P5 subscriber isolation is therefore **best-effort plus lint**: the kernel calls handlers one at a time from its own loop, so an aborted handler does not stop the loop; the sentinel names the offending subscriber in diagnostics; a lint forbids handlers from calling anything that can write.
- **(d) Violations.** A *violation* (write outside a `WriteScope`, a sim read of `PERCEPTION_OUT`, a hook reaching the `PLAYER` ingress, a submit during `SAVING`, a payload that passed the size check but fails the round-trip, a `SIM` hash change at the tripwire) is, in every build: the offending action refused, a named diagnostics counter incremented, `push_error` called. Under `STRICT_DEBUG` the kernel additionally calls the injected `violation_handler(code, detail)`; the dev default halts via `assert(false)`, the test default records. No state-machine outcome (`FAULTED`, reject reasons, results) differs between profiles.
- **(e) KernelProfile.** `KernelProfile` ∈ {`STRICT_DEBUG`, `LENIENT_RELEASE`} is injected at construction (H10) and never read from `OS.is_debug_build()` inside the kernel, so one test process can construct a kernel per profile and exercise both branches. `STRICT_DEBUG` enables only the extras: the per-command serialization round-trip (CR-4), the violation handler, the `SIM` tripwire (CR-12) and the counter test seams.

**Velocity rule (gameplay-programmer, adopted as an acceptance criterion).** Adding a new command verb touches at most two files: one handler and one registration line. If the kernel ever makes a feature cost more than that, the layer will be bypassed — which is the exact lapse TD-FEASIBILITY named. Hence: commands are plain data records (no class per verb), state blocks are coarse (one per domain system, not per entity), and replay/undo/rollback/middleware are deferred.

### States and Transitions

content.content:
# Design Directory

When authoring or editing files in this directory, follow these standards.

## GDD Files (`design/gdd/`)

The 8 GDD sections, in order:
1. Overview — one-paragraph summary
2. Player Fantasy — intended feeling and experience
3. Detailed Rules — unambiguous mechanics
4. Formulas — all math defined with variables
5. Edge Cases — unusual situations handled
6. Dependencies — other systems listed
7. Tuning Knobs — configurable values identified
8. Acceptance Criteria — testable success conditions

**How many are REQUIRED depends on `modes.workflow`** — all 8 at `full`; 5 at
`standard` (Overview, Detailed Rules, Edge Cases, Dependencies, Acceptance
Criteria, plus Formulas when the system has math); none at `minimal`, where
`design/game-brief.md` is the design record instead of a GDD. Resolve the tier
before flagging a section as missing — see `.claude/docs/workflow-modes.md`.

> **Three other places already encode the tier rule** —
> `.claude/docs/coding-standards.md`, `.claude/rules/design-docs.md` and
> `.claude/hooks/validate-commit.sh`. This file is the copy a session working in
> `design/` reads first, so it must agree with them: demanding all 8 at
> `minimal` warns a jam project about six sections its own configuration says it
> does not need, which trains the user to ignore the warning.

**Section-name alias:** the GDD template and `/design-system` author section 3
as `## Detailed Design`; the standard calls it **Detailed Rules**. Same required
section — accept either heading, never rewrite one into the other.

**File naming:** `[system-slug].md` (e.g. `movement-system.md`, `combat-system.md`)

**Systems index:** `design/gdd/systems-index.md` — update when adding a new GDD.

**Design order:** Foundation → Core → Feature → Presentation → Polish

**Validation:** Run `/design-review [path]` after authoring any GDD.
Run `/review-all-gdds` after completing a set of related GDDs.

## Quick Specs (`design/quick-specs/`)

Lightweight specs for tuning changes, minor mechanics, or balance adjustments.
Use `/quick-design` to author.

## UX Specs (`design/ux/`)

- Per-screen specs: `design/ux/[screen-name].md`
- HUD design: `design/ux/hud.md`
- Interaction pattern library: `design/ux/interaction-patterns.md`
- Accessibility requirements: `design/accessibility-requirements.md`

Use `/ux-design` to author. Validate with `/ux-review` before passing to `/team-ui`.

> **Accessibility requirements sit OUTSIDE `design/ux/` on purpose.** They are a
> project-wide standard the per-screen specs consult, not a spec for one screen.
> `.claude/docs/workflow-catalog.yaml`, the Pre-Production, Production and Polish
> gates, and `/architecture-review` all check `design/accessibility-requirements.md`
> at that exact path. Do not "tidy" it under `design/ux/` — every one of those
> checks would stop matching, and the Technical Setup → Pre-Production gate would
> become unpassable. `/ux-design` states the same rule at its `accessibility` mode.
